raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old male, previously infected with COVID-19, has a history of hypertension and pancreatitis. He has a smoking and alcohol consumption habit, with no family history of hereditary diseases, and no history of drug or food allergies. He has received the COVID-19 vaccine before. He was admitted due to a four-day history of headache and two days of dizziness. Prior to admission, he had received ceftriaxone for infection control, amlodipine for blood pressure management, and mannitol for intracranial pressure reduction, but his condition did not improve. Physical examination revealed increased neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign on both sides. Laboratory tests indicated elevated WBC count, increased neutrophil percentage, accelerated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, with all other blood parameters falling within the normal range. Chest CT revealed bronchitis, diffuse fibrous proliferation in both lungs, and mild thickening of the bilateral pleura. The head MRI revealed an acute cerebral infarction adjacent to the left lateral ventricle, as shown in  Figure 2 . accompanied by increased intracranial pressure of 400+ mmHg (normal range: 80-180 mmHg). The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) routine test showed that the appearance was colorless and transparent, with a nucleated cell count of 31/muL. The Pandy test was weakly positive, and the CSF India ink staining indicated the presence of Cryptococcus. Further culture and identification of bacteria and fungi in the CSF revealed the detection of Cryptococcus neoformans. Cryptococcus neoformans was detected in blood culture, as depicted in  Figure 3 . Peripheral blood cultures from both hands were cultured for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. After incubation, no bacterial growth was observed in the anaerobic bottles and one of the aerobic bottles; however, positive growth triggering an alarm was noted in the other aerobic bottle. Gram staining revealed fungal spores, as shown in  Figure 3C . Subsequent subculturing on specific agar mediums confirmed fungal growth and identified a Cryptococcus neoformans strain through mass spectrometry. The patient had a Cryptococcus neoformans infection, ultimately diagnosed as CM. A four-week course of antifungal therapy is being conducted, which includes amphotericin B with flucytosine. In addition, adjunctive therapies such as mannitol, glycerol fructose, and albumin dehydration are being used to reduce intracranial pressure, alleviate symptoms, and prevent certain complications like brain herniation.
On the 16th day of antifungal treatment for Cryptococcal infection, the patient developed fever and symptoms of a pulmonary infection. Upon examination, signs of a lung infection were detected. The patient was initially infected with the novel coronavirus approximately 5 months ago, and they are currently experiencing a surge in secondary COVID-19 infections. Due to the patient's compromised immune system and the potential for secondary infections, the doctor has opted to incorporate a 5-day course of Molnupiravir as part of the antiviral treatment plan. On day 21 of the treatment, the patient developed acute pancreatitis, confirmed by abdominal CT scans. Treatment includes fasting, omeprazole, and somatostatin to control pancreatic enzyme secretion. After completing a 4-week course of treatment for CM, the patient's symptoms showed significant improvement. He has been discharged and will continue treatment at a local hospital. The treatment timelines for Case 1 and Case 2 are shown in  Figure 4 .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of headache and a 2-day history of dizziness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed headache 4 days prior to admission and dizziness 2 days prior to admission. Outpatient treatment with ceftriaxone, amlodipine, and mannitol failed to improve his symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior COVID-19 infection (approximately 5 months prior) and prior COVID-19 vaccination; hypertension; pancreatitis. Positive smoking and alcohol consumption history; no family history of hereditary diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache and dizziness. No drug or food allergies. Pre-admission medications included ceftriaxone, amlodipine, and mannitol.

objective.physical_examination: Increased neck stiffness and bilateral positive Kernig sign.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated WBC count, increased neutrophil percentage, and accelerated ESR, with other routine blood parameters within normal ranges.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT showed bronchitis, bilateral diffuse pulmonary fibrous proliferation, and mild bilateral pleural thickening. Head MRI revealed an acute cerebral infarction adjacent to the left lateral ventricle. Lumbar puncture demonstrated markedly elevated intracranial pressure >400 mmHg (normal: 80-180 mmHg), colorless transparent CSF, nucleated cell count 31/uL, weakly positive Pandy test, positive CSF India ink stain, and positive CSF and aerobic peripheral blood cultures for Cryptococcus neoformans.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis and fungemia complicated by acute left periventricular cerebral infarction, secondary COVID-19 reinfection (day 16), and acute pancreatitis (day 21), confirmed by CSF India ink staining, CSF and blood cultures, and mass spectrometry identification. Treated with a 4-week induction course of amphotericin B plus flucytosine alongside intracranial pressure reduction using mannitol, glycerol fructose, and albumin dehydration. Secondary COVID-19 pulmonary infection on day 16 was treated with a 5-day course of molnupiravir, and CT-confirmed acute pancreatitis on day 21 was managed with fasting, omeprazole, and somatostatin; he improved significantly and was discharged to a local hospital for continuation of therapy.
